title: How to Give a Back Massage: A 15-Minute Step-by-Step Guide — cv.cm
description: How to give a back massage at home: setup, strokes in order, pressure beside the spine, a 15-minute sequence, giver posture and lower back self-massage.
h1: How do you give a good back massage?
answer: Have the person lie face down on a firm bed with a pillow under the ankles and a towel over the body. Warm oil in your hands, glide up both sides of the spine, knead the muscles two finger-widths beside it, work around the shoulder blades and the lower back, then finish with long gliding strokes. Never press on the spine itself.

sections.h: Set up: surface, towel, oil and position
body: This guide is for massaging a family member or friend, who stays clothed or covered with a towel or sheet. A calm, warm setup makes the massage work better than any technique.

ul: Surface: a firm bed, or a thick folded blanket on the floor. A soft mattress absorbs your pressure.
Room: warm, about 22–25 °C, with no draft.

Position: the person lies face down with arms by the sides or bent loosely beside the head. A pillow under the ankles relaxes the lower back. A pillow under the hips helps if lying flat is uncomfortable. A rolled towel under the forehead keeps the neck straight.
If lying face down is not comfortable, the person can sit backward on a chair, leaning on a pillow over the chair back, or lie on one side with a pillow between the knees.
Towel: cover the body and fold it down to the waist to uncover the back. Keep the towel tucked at the waistband.
Oil or lotion: about a teaspoon of plain, unscented oil or lotion, warmed in your palms. Add more only when your hands start to drag.

body: Before you begin, ask about back pain, injuries, recent surgery, osteoporosis, blood thinners and skin problems. If any apply, read our page on when not to massage first.

sections.h: Where to press and where never to press
body: The long muscles that run up the back lie in two ridges on each side of the spine. You can feel them as firm bands about one to three finger-widths beside the bumps of the spine. That is where most of your work goes.

head: Area
How to find it
What to do
Pressure (1–10)
rows: The firm ridge two finger-widths out from the bony bumps of the spine
Glide and knead from the waist to the neck
The thick muscle between the neck and the point of the shoulder
The flat triangle bones on the upper back; feel for their inner edge
Small thumb circles along the muscle next to the inner edge, not on the bone
The area between the bottom ribs and the top of the hip bones
Flat palm circles and gentle kneading at the sides

The bony center line and the soft area just below the last ribs
Do not press. Only glide lightly over them

body.note: Never press, push or try to crack the spine. Keep your thumbs off the bony bumps in the center, and use only light gliding over the lower ribs and the area just below them.

body: Time each step so you cover the whole back. For example, cv.cm's countdown timer can run a 15-minute session or each step in turn.

head: Step
What to do
Time
rows: Rest both palms flat on the upper back for three slow breaths. Agree on 'more', 'less' and 'stop'.
Hands flat on each side of the spine at the waist. Glide up to the neck, out across the shoulders, and lightly down the sides. Repeat slowly.
Overlap both hands and make slow circles on the muscles on one side of the spine, moving from the lower back up to the shoulder blade. Then the other side.
Squeeze and lift the muscles beside the spine, hand over hand, waist to shoulders, one side then the other.
Rest one of the person's hands on their lower back if comfortable, so the blade lifts slightly. Make small thumb circles along its inner edge. Both sides.
Knead the thick muscle between neck and shoulder. Ask about pressure here, it is often tender.
Slow palm circles on both sides of the lower back, then gentle kneading at the waist.
Long, slow gliding strokes over the whole back, getting lighter each time, then 20 s of light tapping on the upper back if liked. Cover with the towel.

body: Move at about one long stroke every 3–4 seconds. Keep one hand on the back as you change position so the person is not surprised by your touch.
A back massage can strain your own back, wrists and thumbs. Work smart:

ul: Stand or kneel close to the person so you do not reach far. If the person is on a low bed, kneel on a cushion beside it.
Keep your back straight and bend at the hips and knees, not at the waist.
Get pressure by leaning your body weight forward slowly, with straight arms, not by squeezing hard with your hands.
Use your palms and the heel of your hand most of the time. Rest your thumbs every minute or two.
Change sides of the bed to work each side of the back, instead of reaching across.

body: You cannot reach your own back well with your hands, so use simple tools.

ol: Ball against a wall, 3 minutes: place a tennis ball between the wall and the muscle beside your spine, never on the spine itself. Bend your knees slowly to roll the ball up and down 5–10 cm. Pause 20–30 seconds on a tender spot, at a pressure of 4–5 out of 10.
Hands on the waist, 1 minute: put your hands on your hips with thumbs toward the back and make slow thumb circles in the muscles beside the spine.

Foam roller for the upper and middle back, 2 minutes: lie on the roller across the upper back, hands behind your head, and roll slowly between the shoulder blades and the bottom of the ribs. Do not roll the lower back on a foam roller. Use the ball against the wall instead.
Gentle movement: after massage, walk for a few minutes or do gentle back stretches.

body: The NHS advises that keeping active, using heat for stiffness or an ice pack wrapped in a towel, and doing back exercises and stretches can help with everyday back pain. Stop any exercise that makes the pain worse.

A 2015 Cochrane review of massage for low back pain looked at 25 trials. It found that massage improved pain in the short term compared with no treatment or a fake treatment, but the improvement did not last. The authors said they had very little confidence that massage is an effective treatment for low back pain. The side effects reported were minor, mostly a short increase in pain.
NCCIH describes the evidence for massage and low back pain as weak. In practice, a back massage may help a person relax and feel less tense for a while. It is not a treatment for a back condition.

sections.h: Lower back red flags and when to stop
body: Stop the massage if it causes sharp, shooting or burning pain, or pain that spreads into a leg. Mild tenderness the next day is common; if so, halve the pressure next time.
Get emergency care, according to the NHS, if back pain comes with any of these:

ul: Numbness or loss of feeling around the genitals, anus or inner thighs.
Difficulty peeing, or loss of bladder or bowel control.
Pain, tingling, weakness or numbness in both legs.
Pain that started after a serious accident or fall.

body: Get an urgent doctor's appointment if back pain comes with fever, chills or feeling generally unwell, or if severe pain starts suddenly or gets worse quickly. Also see a doctor if back pain has not improved after a few weeks, if you have a history of cancer, or if you have osteoporosis. Do not massage the back of someone with a fever, fresh injury or recent spine surgery.

faq.q: Should you massage the lower back when it hurts?
faq.a: Gentle massage beside the spine may help some people relax and feel less stiff. Stop if it causes sharp or spreading pain, and see a doctor for back pain with any red-flag signs or that does not improve.

faq.q: Is it OK to press on the spine during a back massage?
faq.a: No. Press only on the muscles beside the spine, and only glide lightly over the bony center line. Never push down on the spine or try to crack it.

faq.q: How long should a back massage last?
faq.a: 10–20 minutes is enough for a home back massage. About 2–3 minutes per area keeps the massage even and avoids soreness from too much work on one spot.

faq.q: What is the best position for a back massage at home?
faq.a: Lying face down on a firm bed with a pillow under the ankles works best. If that is uncomfortable, sitting backward on a chair and leaning on a pillow, or lying on one side, are good options.

faq.q: Can I use a foam roller on my lower back?
faq.a: It is better not to. Use a foam roller on the upper and middle back only, and use a ball against the wall beside the spine for the lower back.
